query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The magnetocaloric response and hysteresis in as‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys are primarily governed by the internal microstructure—specifically the density of grain boundaries and associated interfacial strain—which strongly influences the coupling between the magnetic and structural transitions. By intentionally refining the grain size and thus increasing the surface-to-volume ratio (and grain-boundary density) through a controlled high-energy ball-milling intervention, the internal strain barriers that typically lead to a sharp, hysteretic, first-order magnetostructural transition will be partially relaxed. This microstructural modification is anticipated to reduce hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles while still maintaining a sizable magnetocaloric entropy change.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy in bulk form characterized by a relatively coarse-grained, ordered single-phase hexagonal structure exhibiting a strongly coupled first-order magnetostructural transition with pronounced thermal and magnetic hysteresis.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled high-energy ball-milling process to reduce the grain size into the nanostructured regime (roughly 20–100 nm), thereby increasing the grain-boundary density and modifying the internal stress distribution without altering the overall phase (hexagonal) or composition.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles near the magnetostructural transition temperature (e.g., within a few tesla and the temperature range where the as-deposited alloy exhibits its peak response). Structural characterization via XRD/TEM and thermal/magnetic measurements (DSC, M vs. T, and ΔSM determination) are to be measured at and around this transition temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The increased grain-boundary area and the reduction of internal strain fields act as mediators by easing the nucleation and propagation of the magnetostructural transition, thereby smoothing the transformation kinetics.
generation.mechanism: High-energy ball milling refines the microstructure, which in turn relaxes internal stresses and reduces the elastic constraint at grain boundaries. This reduced constraint lowers the energy barriers for the transition and allows for more homogeneous nucleation of the structural change. Consequently, the latent heat and hysteresis associated with the sharp first-order transition are reduced, while the increased surface-to-volume ratio enhances the heat-exchange rate during magnetic-cooling cycles.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the coarse-grained, as-deposited baseline, the nanostructured alloy will exhibit a reduced hysteresis width during low-field magnetization/demagnetization cycles and a somewhat broadened magnetocaloric response (with a modest decrease in the peak entropy change) but with improved heat exchange and cycle efficiency.
generation.baseline: As-deposited bulk alloy with larger grain sizes, a single-phase hexagonal structure, a strongly first-order magnetostructural transition, large latent heat, and significant hysteresis during magnetic-cooling cycles.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected when the grain size is reduced into the mid–nanoscale regime (approximately 20–100 nm) while keeping the single-phase hexagonal structure intact; the effects should be observable under low-applied magnetic fields (on the order of a few tesla) near the intrinsic transition temperature. Outside these processing or field/temperature regimes, the intervention may either not yield the predicted hysteresis reduction or may excessively dilute the magnetocaloric effect.
generation.uncertainty: The trade-off between reducing hysteresis and maintaining a high peak entropy change is not precisely known. It is also uncertain whether the induced nanostructuring might introduce deleterious defects that compromise mechanical stability or the long-term reversibility of the transition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy samples: one set remains as-deposited (bulk, coarse-grained) and the other set is subjected to a controlled high-energy ball-milling treatment to achieve nanostructured grain sizes (20–100 nm). Conduct identical thermal and magnetic measurements under low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles near the transition temperature. Structural characterization (by XRD and TEM) will confirm the grain size distribution and phase stability. The thermal hysteresis will be evaluated using DSC and the magnetic transition behavior using low-field M versus T measurements, alongside ΔSM determination.
measurements: Grain size and phase confirmation via XRD and TEM
DSC curves to extract thermal hysteresis and latent heat
Magnetization versus temperature (M(T)) curves to assess magnetic hysteresis
Magnetic entropy change (ΔSM) determination from isothermal magnetization measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanostructured samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis width compared to the as-deposited baseline or if the magnetocaloric entropy change is reduced beyond acceptable performance thresholds (i.e., a drastic loss in ΔSM), then the hypothesis that internal microstructure and grain-boundary strain mediate the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis is rejected.
